title: The men who measured him used a different ruler than you're picturing.
description:
The men who measured him used a different ruler than you're picturing. His valet, a general and his own physician all recorded the same figure: five pieds, two pouces. That is French feet and inches, not English ones.

He comes out at roughly five foot six. A French pouce measured 2.7 centimetres against the English inch's 2.54. Do the sum and Napoleon lands just under 5'6", a little above the average French man of his time.

British cartoonist who invented 'Little Boney', a diminutive, raving caricature of Napoleon, in response to a real outburst the emperor made at the British ambassador on 14 March 1803. Gillray kept shrinking him for years afterwards.

By 1804 he was drawn six inches tall. Gillray's cartoons showed Napoleon as an animal, then a baby, then a Lilliputian dwarfed by an English giant in 'The King of Brobdingnag and Gulliver'. The caricature, not the ruler, is what stuck.

Napoleon himself said Gillray 'did more than all the armies of Europe to bring me down'.

Sources:
- https://www.history.com/articles/napoleon-complex-short - HISTORY (Una McIlvenna, 13 November 2019, updated 10 July 2025), read in full. Established that three French sources, Napoleon's valet Constant, General Gourgaud and his physician Francesco Antommarchi, recorded his height as '5 pieds 2 pouces'; that the French pouce measured 2.7cm against the imperial inch's 2.54cm, so the true figure converts to roughly 1.67 metres, just under 5'6", a little above the average French man of the early 1800s; that the 'short Napoleon' image is largely the work of British cartoonist James Gillray (1756-1815); that Gillray's earliest Napoleon cartoons (1798) showed him boastful but not small; that the diminutive 'Little Boney' image began with Gillray's 1803 cartoon 'Maniac-Ravings, or Little Boney in a Strong Fit', satirising a real outburst by Napoleon against the British ambassador, Lord Whitworth, at the Tuileries on 14 March 1803; that Gillray's 1805 cartoon 'The Plumb-pudding in Danger', described as probably the most famous political cartoon of all time, shows Napoleon at half the size of British Prime Minister William Pitt the Younger; and that Napoleon reportedly said Gillray 'did more than all the armies of Europe to bring me down'.
- https://publicdomainreview.org/essay/little-boney/ - The Public Domain Review (Peter W. Walker, Assistant Professor of History, University of Wyoming, 21 March 2024), read in full. Established that Gillray produced around forty of the more than two thousand British satirical prints of Napoleon and that his were the most influential; that Gillray's 1798 cartoon still drew Napoleon as 'average-sized'; that the caricature shrank progressively through 1803 as invasion fears grew, becoming an animal in 'Death of the Corsican Fox', a baby in 'The Genius of France', and a six-inch Lilliputian dwarfed by an English giant in 'The King of Brobdingnag and Gulliver' (1804); that other cartoonists copied the trope; and that the term 'Napoleon Complex' derives directly from this caricature legacy and is described as being of questionable scientific validity.
